cards.title: Creative-as-Targeting: Structuring Meta Ad Sets by Concept
cards.summary: Under Meta's Andromeda system the creative itself does the targeting, so each ad set should hold one concept (persona + angle + offer) rather than a mix.
cards.use_when: Setting up or restructuring Meta ad campaigns and deciding what goes inside each ad set.
steps: Accept the mechanical shift the source describes: pre-Andromeda you picked interests and loaded creatives underneath them; post-Andromeda you load creatives with broad (or no) targeting and Meta reads transcripts, copy and visuals to decide who to show them to. The creative is the targeting.

Because targeting largely lives at the ad set level, put only one concept per ad set. A concept = persona + angle + offer. If you bundle several concepts into one ad set, the ad set cannot resolve who it is for and performance degrades.
Define each ad set so its ads all call out the same kind of person, agitate the same problem and present the same argument.
Diversify across ad sets instead of within them: three ads in one ad set should talk to three different people (different concepts), not three near-identical edits of the same shoot.
Reason the source gives: unique concepts reach their own audiences, so frequency stays low on cold traffic and you can scale into colder audiences without efficiency collapsing.
Verify the current Ads Manager interface and any similarity/bundling reporting available to your account before restructuring, since Meta's tooling changes.
caveats: The source describes Andromeda behavior as of the recording; Meta's algorithm and interface change, so re-verify.
Some ad-level audience siloing exists, but the presenter argues most targeting still sits at the ad set level.

cards.title: Diagnose Frequency Above 2 on Cold Ads as a Fatigue Red Flag
cards.summary: Cold-traffic ads should rarely exceed frequency 2; if they do you likely lack creative diversity or volume rather than needing a media-buying fix.
cards.use_when: Weekly or monthly ad account health check, deciding whether to produce more creative or change campaign setup.
steps: Pull the account to the ad level and filter to cold/prospecting campaigns over the last 30–60 days.
Look at frequency per cold ad. The source's rule of thumb: cold ads should almost never show frequency above 2. If they do, treat it as a red flag, not a normal condition.

If frequency is high, diagnose it as insufficient concept diversity and volume, not as a bidding or targeting problem to fix with media-buying levers. The fix is new concepts and formats entering the account.

Support the diagnosis with the source's citation of a Meta article (roughly four to five years old at time of recording) stating the probability of purchase falls sharply after about two impressions of an identical creative, but stays high when a novel creative is introduced instead.
Act by adding differentiated concepts at the ad set level and new formats, then re-check frequency after the new assets have had time to run.
caveats: The frequency-2 threshold is the presenter's heuristic for cold campaigns, not a universal rule for all account types or warm/retargeting audiences.
The referenced Meta article's exact wording and current availability should be verified.

cards.title: Creative Portfolio Model: Avoid Over-Levering Into One or Two Ads
cards.summary: Spread spend across many ads rather than one or two heroes, because every creative eventually fatigues and no single ad holds unlimited spend.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much of total spend to concentrate in top-performing ads and whether to keep funding creative production.
steps: Frame the account as two scenarios at the same $1,000/day and same blended 4x: one creative holding the entire budget versus three creatives splitting it. The source prefers the three-creative version because any one ad can fatigue while the others absorb spend and maintain efficiency.
Accept the premise that every creative eventually fatigues and has a maximum spend threshold, so concentration is a delayed liability, not a win.

Watch for the pattern the source describes from client experience: brands built eight-figure businesses on a handful of creatives that held large spend, stopped producing, then faced 40%+ year-over-year declines in new customer acquisition when those ads fatigued. The source says this is typically fixable 6–8 months earlier, not at the moment of decline.
Set the operating goal as many ads holding as much spend as possible, and keep feeding the portfolio even when current winners are hitting KPI.
Allocate budget to creative production as a revenue driver, not a cost center — the source treats the creative, not the platform, as the engine and Meta as distribution.
caveats: The 4x and $1,000/day figures are illustrative, not benchmarks.
The 40% decline and 6–8 month window are case-study observations from the presenter's clients, not measured averages.

cards.title: Use Amount Spent as the Ad-Level Proxy for Creative Performance
cards.summary: At the ad level judge creatives by how much spend Meta allocates to them, because in-platform ROAS at the ad level is distorted by last-click attribution.
cards.use_when: Reviewing the ad-level table in Ads Manager to decide which creatives are working.
steps: Understand that Meta optimizes distribution using multi-touch sequencing (multi-click and view), but reports ROAS on last-click. So the ad that gets credited with the purchase may only be the closer, while earlier ads did the persuasion work.

Read the ad-level ROAS column with skepticism. A 6x closer ad does not mean the 1.4x opener ad is useless — the source says turning off the low-ROAS opener destroys performance when the sequence was working.
Treat Amount Spent as the better ad-level signal: if Meta is allocating spend to a creative, it is because the system believes that creative contributes to conversions across the sequence.
Use this to avoid the mistake of killing 'underperforming' ads that are actually doing top-of-funnel work.
Verify the current Ads Manager columns and any multi-touch reporting options available, since these change.
caveats: Amount Spent is a proxy, not proof of incrementality. The source says there is no direct visibility into Meta's multi-touch sequencing.
Ad-level ROAS is not useless when you have no better data; it just should not be the primary decision metric for creative sequencing.

cards.title: Measure ROAS at Ad Set and Campaign Level, Not the Ad Level
cards.summary: Reliability of ROAS improves as you move up the account structure from ad to ad set to campaign, so make optimisation decisions higher up.
cards.use_when: Deciding which level of the account to base budget and creative decisions on.
steps: Rank reliability: ad-level ROAS is the least trustworthy because of last-click attribution and multi-touch journeys; ad-set-level ROAS groups the sequenced ads and is more reliable for evaluating a concept; campaign-level ROAS on 7-day click (with existing customers excluded) is the most reliable and tends to be congruent with the P&L.
Use the ad set as your concept-level scorecard. If one concept per ad set is working at the ad-set level, you can confidently say the concept works and make more like it.

Note the caveat the source flags: some cross-ad-set serving still occurs, so one ad set can pick up bottom-of-funnel conversions generated by another. Keep concepts diversified across ad sets, and measure the overlap, to reduce this.
Make structuring and creative-introduction decisions using ad-set and campaign numbers, and use ad-level numbers only as secondary context.
caveats: Campaign-level reliability depends on 7-day click attribution and excluding existing customers; other settings change the interpretation.
Cross-ad-set overlap is possible and can make individual ad sets look better than they are.

cards.title: The Concept Framework: Persona, Angle, Offer (and Format)
cards.summary: A concept is a persona, an angle, and an offer; changing any one of the three produces genuinely different targeting.
cards.use_when: Ideating the next batch of ads or auditing whether recent ads were actually different from each other.
steps: Define concept as persona + angle + offer. Two ads only count as different concepts if at least one of these three changes.
Persona: think about who you are talking to AND who is in the ad. A 60-year-old woman in the ad versus a 20-year-old woman will reach different people even with the same product.
Angle: the problem you agitate and the argument you make. Skincare agitating wrinkles versus agitating hormonal acne reaches two different audiences with the same product.
Offer: the product itself and how value is framed (bundles, gifts with purchase, subscriptions, tiered discounts).

Add format as a fourth, weaker variable: with the same persona, angle and offer, changing format can reach some new people (e.g. people who never click UGC), but it hits largely the same audience. Rank it last.
Naming convention and ideation sheets should encode persona/angle/offer so you can see at a glance whether new ads are genuinely new concepts.
caveats: Format is the source's lowest-priority lever for novelty; do not treat a format swap as a new concept.
Some brands can make very broad unaware ads work, but the source says that requires high skill and is not needed for most accounts.

cards.title: Testing Priority Order: Angle First, Then Offer, Persona, Format
cards.summary: When creative isn't working, fix angle first, then offer, then persona, and test format last.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why ads are underperforming and deciding what variable to test next.
steps: Rank the four levers in the source's order: (1) angle, (2) offer, (3) persona, (4) format. The source says most teams invert this and spend all their time testing formats.
Angle first: if you are targeting personas who already purchase from you, and they still aren't buying, the problem is message or argument. Rotate and improve the angle.

Offer second: it may be the single most important variable, but flexibility is limited. With one or two products you cannot change the product, and offer variants (bundles, gift with purchase, tiered discounts, subscriptions) eventually run out. The source warns against solving this with heavy discounts that eat margin and create discount dependence.
Persona third: it is mainly what gives you breadth and volume once angle and offer are dialled in.
Format last: 'UGC doesn't work' is the wrong lesson — the script, persona, angle and offer inside the format are what work. Same for professional photo shoots.
caveats: The source treats the ranking as a practical heuristic, not an absolute law, and notes offer is arguably the most important variable in theory.
The claim that most accounts do not need broad-audience unaware ads is the presenter's opinion based on their client experience.

cards.title: Build Sharp Personas From Problems, Not Demographics
cards.summary: Use specific problem-defined archetypes rather than age/gender bands, because broad personas produce forgettable, unscalable creative.
cards.use_when: Writing creative briefs and deciding who each new ad is speaking to.
steps: Define personas as archetypes defined by problems, desires and buying triggers — not as demographics. Reject 'women 25–45' or 'busy professional' as too broad.

Sharpen to a concrete situation. Fashion example: not 'busy professional' but 'a consultant who flies twice a week and needs a carry-on wardrobe that works for boardrooms and bars'. Supplement example: not 'health-conscious parent' but 'a mom who's tried six different supplements because her toddler won't eat vegetables'.
For each persona, capture the pains, the language used to talk to them, and the proof they need. These three things determine the brief, the script, the casting and the visuals.
Expect breadth from depth: the source argues five ads for one sharp persona will beat five ads for a broad audience until you are a large eight-figure brand with the skill to run broad unaware ads.

Use age/gender only as a starting split, then immediately subdivide by the underlying problem. Acne at 20-25, acne at 30-35 (possibly hormonal) and acne at 40-45 are three distinct problems and three distinct personas.
caveats: Fair, the source is presenter opinion based on client work, not measured lift.
Ultra-broad unaware ads can work for large brands — that is a different, higher-skill play, not a contradiction.

cards.title: Scale Persona Ideation Manually, Then Use LLMs to Expand
cards.summary: Do 20–40 sharp personas manually first, then use an LLM with heavy context to expand, and curate the output back down.
cards.use_when: Building a persona library for creative ideation.
steps: Spend focused manual time (the source suggests ~20 minutes of hard thinking) listing personas and the problems/desires/triggers behind each.
Take the manually built list (20–40 personas) and give it to an LLM along with as much business and target-demographic context as possible. Ask for 20–30 more.
The source warns LLMs default to averages: if you only give it three or four personas plus your website, you get a mean-reverting, generic list that everyone else also gets.
Curate the LLM output. Of ~20 generated personas, keep the four or five strongest and feed those back with a request for 10–20 more. Use this loop to roughly double the library.
Reject any persona on the list that is broad (e.g. 'women 25–45') — broad personas produce mediocre creative.
caveats: LLM persona output is starting material, not finished work; the source says curation is mandatory.
The 20–40 and 20–30 figures are the source's suggested working amounts, not measured benchmarks.

cards.title: Angle Playbook: Problem Agitation, Contrarian Truth, Curiosity Gap, Proof, Comparison, Transformation
cards.summary: Assemble angles from a known set of persuasive components rather than defaulting to product features.
cards.use_when: Writing ad scripts or deciding what the next angle variant should be.
steps: Lead with pain where possible: make the viewer feel the problem and feel heard before introducing the solution. The source notes you cannot problem-agitate someone who isn't problem-aware, so this is not universal.
Contrarian truth: challenge a common belief to reframe, e.g. 'everything you've been told about X is wrong', then educate.

Curiosity gap: open with an information gap (e.g. 'here's what the top 1% of millionaires know about saving money that they don't want you to know') and delay the answer, holding attention through problem agitation and story before paying it off.

Social proof and domain authority: use proof specific to the persona and the domain — a marathon runner for a running product, a clinical study for a creatine energy claim aimed at 40–45-year-old women.
Comparison and objection handling: acknowledge what the viewer has already tried and why this works differently. UGC scripts often narrate 'I tried X, it didn't work, then I tried this'.
Transformation / before-after: the source calls it the best-performing component but the least compliant; it must be worked in so the platform doesn't flag it.
Simplify the angle into a one-sentence claim (persona → product → argument), then expand it into a script.
caveats: Before-after ads are called out as non-compliant; the source describes sneaking them in, which carries platform and policy risk — treat compliance as your responsibility.
The source says not every angle needs every component; choose elements that fit the persona's awareness level.

cards.title: Write Hooks That Call Out a Real Persona With a Real Pain
cards.summary: Hooks drive persona targeting on Meta, so a badly aimed call-out pushes your ad to irrelevant people.
cards.use_when: Producing hooks and opening seconds for video ads.
steps: Understand that Meta auto-transcribes every ad and uses transcript content to find the audience. A hook that says 'if you're a business owner doing over $5M a year' will make the system hunt for that audience.
Check your hook actually matches your buyer. If the call-out names a persona that is not your audience, you have pushed distribution toward irrelevant people.
Pair the persona call-out with problem agitation. The source's most common criticism is creators call out a persona without agitating the problem, producing a weak hook.
Keep the call-out specific (see the persona card) so the system has a clear signal about who to find.
Treat hooks as one of the highest-leverage creative elements under Andromeda, alongside volume and concept diversity.
caveats: The transcription-and-targeting mechanism is the source's explanation of Andromeda behaviour and may change; verify current behaviour.
'Most ads I see are not good' is the presenter's qualitative opinion, not a measured failure rate.

cards.title: Stop Confusing Creative Activity for Creative Strategy
cards.summary: Launching thousands of ads a month without quality and a point of view wastes budget and signals a misdiagnosed bottleneck.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly creative production volume and output quality.
steps: Check whether volume is producing scale. The source describes two accounts launching 2,000+ new ads per month that could barely hold $4M/month in spend and were unprofitable — evidence the constraint was not volume.

Diagnose which bottleneck is actually limiting you before adding more ads. Candidate creative bottlenecks the source lists: creative quality, format diversification, insufficient top-of-funnel/awareness assets, and failure to use partnership ads or other distribution unlocks.

Fix the diagnosed bottleneck rather than adding activity to a constraint you have not identified. The source's example: increasing sheer volume when the real problem was quality or funnel-stage mix does nothing.
Set a quality bar alongside volume. The source supports launching as many ads as possible but only with a quality standard and a strategy behind the batch.
caveats: The 2,000 ads/month and $4M/month figures are specific case examples, not benchmarks.
The source does not give a numeric ads-per-month target — it explicitly rejects a simple volume formula.

cards.title: Include Creative Production in the Media Budget at 10–25%
cards.summary: The source recommends dedicating roughly 10–25% of media spend to creative production to sustain the volume needed against fatigue.
cards.use_when: Setting or defending the creative production budget for the coming quarter.
steps: Decide creative production as a percentage of media spend rather than a flat fee. The source's stated benchmark: about 25% of media spend for brands spending $30K–$100K per month, scaling down to about 10% for brands spending over $100K per month.
Also hold a minimum allocation of 10–25% of total media budget to creative production so you can maintain the volume required to combat ad fatigue.

Treat this as an investment in the revenue driver, not a cost to minimise. The source's argument: the creative is what drives revenue; Meta and other platforms only drive distribution, and the same creative can also earn free distribution organically.
Compare your current production spend against this band to see if you are under- or over-investing.
caveats: These percentages are the source's recommended benchmarks, not measured results; they should be adjusted to category, margin and asset types.
The bands ($30K–$100K, over $100K) are the source's stated spend brackets, not derived from an audited study.

cards.title: Do Not Switch Off a Creative That Is Hitting Ad Set KPI
cards.summary: Meta sequences creatives across a purchase journey and optimises on multi-touch, so low ad-level ROAS can be the opener doing the work.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pause the 'underperforming' ads in a working ad set.
steps: Before pausing, look at the ad set level. If the ad set is hitting your overall performance goal, the source says leave the creatives alone.

If you can read the creatives, infer the likely sequence: an unaware top-of-funnel asset usually opens, a product-aware asset sits in the middle, and a very bottom-of-funnel asset closes. The closer often shows the highest ad-level ROAS while the opener shows the lowest.
Recognise that Meta's optimisation is multi-click and view based, so it allocates spend to the opener knowing it contributed, while reporting all revenue to the closer under last-click.
Avoid the trap of turning off the opener because its ad-level ROAS looks weak — the source says this destroys performance.
If you cannot read the sequence from the assets, rely on the ad-set-level number rather than ad-level ROAS.
caveats: Attribution visibility into Meta's multi-touch sequencing is not available in Ads Manager, so this relies on trusting the system.
The 6x/2x/1.4x figures are illustrative examples from the source, not benchmarks.

cards.title: Creative Fatigue Is Structural: Build for Obsolescence From Day One
cards.summary: Every creative has a maximum spend ceiling and will fatigue, so plan replacement before decline rather than after.
cards.use_when: Planning the creative roadmap for a scaling account and deciding how far ahead to produce.
steps: Accept as a planning premise that every creative fatigues and every creative has a maximum spend threshold — there is no permanent winner.
Treat a drop in a previously strong ad as expected, not as an anomaly, and have replacement concepts already in the account or pipeline.

Watch the failure pattern the source describes: brands hit by year-over-year new-customer declines of around 40% after building on a small number of high-spend creatives, arriving when corrective work is already 6–8 months late.
Use the portfolio approach (many ads holding spend) and the 10–25% creative production budget as the structural defences.
Benchmark per-ad spend capacity. The source cites mean ad spend per ad unit landing around $700–$1,500 depending on the account, meaning volume is needed to carry the total budget.
caveats: The $700–$1,500 average ad spend figure is the source's observation across accounts, not a universal benchmark; it will differ by account and objective.
The 40% decline and 6–8 month window are case-study observations.

cards.title: Format Diversity Is Needed to Reach People Meta Won't Show Certain Formats
cards.summary: Meta suppresses formats a user does not engage with, so a single-format account cannot reach everyone.
cards.use_when: Deciding the format mix for a new batch of ads or auditing why reach has plateaued.
steps: Assume Meta learns individual format preferences and stops serving formats people do not click. The source's personal example: he never sees UGC or dynamic product ads (DPAs) in his feed because he does not click them.
If your account runs only UGC, or only UGC plus DPA, you are invisible to users like him regardless of how good the persona and angle are.
Build format variety into the account so the same concept can be delivered to people who respond to different formats.
Expect only incremental new reach from a format swap, not a breakthrough. The source ranks format fourth in the testing priority order because it does not change who the message is for.
Audit reach and frequency by format, and check the current Meta reporting interface for available format breakdowns.
caveats: The presenter's own feed experience is an anecdote, not a measured audience study.
Meta's format-serving behaviour and any DPA/format reporting change over time; verify before making firm conclusions.

cards.title: Escape Interest Targeting Without Lobbing Everyone Into One Broad Bucket
cards.summary: Broad targeting works because the creative does the targeting, but weak or generic creative then gets pushed to the whole population.
cards.use_when: Setting audience targeting in Meta and writing the call-outs that steer it.
steps: Run broadly for the vast majority of accounts — the source recommends roughly 99% of people run broad, and says interest targeting has been effectively dead in their accounts for around two years.
Understand why: labelling people with an interest and serving all creatives to that label ignores the age, psychographic and behavioural nuance that actually predicts purchase.
Recognise the downside of vague creative under broad targeting. If every ad says 'hey everyone, look at this', Meta has no subset to aim at and may serve across the whole population.
Give the algorithm a clear persona signal in the creative so broad targeting still resolves to a defined audience.
Keep one concept per ad set so the ad set is not asked to serve multiple contradictory personas.
caveats: Interest targeting can still make sense in narrow situations; the source's recommendation is directional, and '99%' is the presenter's estimate.
Verify current Meta targeting options before changing account structure.

The source ranks format fourth in the testing priority order because it does not change who the message is for.","Audit reach and frequency by format, and check the current Meta reporting interface for available format breakdowns."],"caveats":["The presenter's own feed experience is an anecdote, not a measured audience study.","Meta's format-serving behaviour and any DPA/format reporting change over time; verify before making firm conclusions."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","formats","creative-strategy","reach","meta-ads","ugc"]},{"title":"Escape Interest Targeting Without Lobbing Everyone Into One Broad Bucket","summary":"Broad targeting works because the creative does the targeting, but weak or generic creative then gets pushed to the whole population.","use_when":"Setting audience targeting in Meta and writing the call-outs that steer it.","steps":["Run broadly for the vast majority of accounts — the source recommends roughly 99% of people run broad, and says interest targeting has been effectively dead in their accounts for around two years.","Understand why: labelling people with an interest and serving all creatives to that label ignores the age, psychographic and behavioural nuance that actually predicts purchase.","Recognise the downside of vague creative under broad targeting.
